file_lines.section: 1.6 *Ashan* H6225 "smoke" (6 verses), *meribah* H4809H / H4808, and the remaining single-verse words
file_lines.text: - ***Ashan*.** The anger word is **literally smoke**: Sinai "wrapped in smoke" (Exo 19:18), and mountains that "smoke" at his touch (Psa 104:32; 144:5). Where it is anger, it is **divine anger answering a human heart**. In Deu 29:20, "the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will smoke against that man". The man is described in 29:18–19: one "whose heart is turning away … blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'". **The seat in the passage is the human's secret self-blessing, and the anger answers it.**

verses.text: Then Hezekiah said, “You have now consecrated yourselves to the Lord. Come near; bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the Lord.” And the assembly brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings.

observations.text: In 2Chr 29:31 and 2Chr 33:16 'thank offerings'/'thanksgiving' sit squarely within todah's cultic-sacrificial base gloss with no notable shift.

In 2Chr 29:31, todah (thank offerings) co-occurs with M22 (glory-related 'said'), M23/M72 (consecrated), M44 (assembly), M09/M34 (willing), M47 (heart), M36 (burnt offerings). Todah's own contribution: it names the specific sacrificial category the consecrated assembly brings, standing alongside but distinct from the burnt offerings (M36) which serve full dedication rather than gratitude.

In 2Chr 29:31 the operation-words 'bring'/'brought' (H0935P, role-T3) are initiated by Hezekiah's assembly, directed toward the house of the Lord, carrying todah offerings as the object of the action.

Across its full occurrence list H8426 clusters into three recurring realizations of one lexeme: (1) the concrete thank-offering sacrifice (Lev.7.12 x2, Lev.7.13, Lev.7.15, Lev.22.29, Ps.50.14, Ps.50.23, Ps.107.22, Ps.116.17, Amos.4.5, Jonah.2.9, 2Chr.29.31 x2, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11), (2) the vocal/manner accompaniment of praise, 'with/in thanksgiving' (Ps.69.30, Ps.26.7, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Isa.51.3), and (3) the institutional thanksgiving choir/procession/company (Neh.12.27, Neh.12.31, Neh.12.38, Neh.12.40, Ps.42.4). A fourth, rarer sense realizes it as verbal confession (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11). This is a single strong showing internally the full sense-range attributed to the subgroup label (hymn, choir, offering) without needing a second member strong to supply any of these senses.

Since H8426 is the sole member strong of this subgroup, there is no second lexeme to compare it against directly; the meaningful cross-comparison available is internal -- between H8426's own sacrificial/cultic-object occurrences (e.g. Lev.7.12-15, Lev.22.29, 2Chr.29.31, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11, Amos.4.5) versus its choir/procession-as-institution occurrences (Neh.12.27-40, Ps.42.4) versus its purely adverbial/manner occurrences ('with thanksgiving', e.g. Ps.69.30, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Ps.26.7). These three groupings do not overlap grammatically: the sacrificial sense is always the head noun or a construct-genitive qualifier of an offering-word (zebach, shelamim), the choir sense functions as a collective-body noun (subject or object of appointment/movement verbs), and the manner sense is marked by a preposition (b-) modifying a separate main verb of praise. No morphological distinction (all occurrences are the same feminine noun stem, singular or plural absolute/construct) drives this three-way split -- it is purely syntactic/contextual, meaning the noun's referent is disambiguated entirely by its syntactic role in each verse rather than by any inflectional change.

Todah takes hold rightly under conditions of a willing heart (2Chr.29.31, 'all who were of a willing heart') and right ordering of one's way of life (Ps.50.23, 'to one who orders his way rightly'); it operates rightly when accompanied by genuine acknowledgment rather than mere ritual performance.

The human-to-God movement of todah requires an inner posture of humility and right-ordering ('to one who orders his way rightly,' Ps.50.23), willingness ('willing heart,' 2Chr.29.31), and honest acknowledgment (confession, Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11) rather than mere external ritual performance.

2Chr.29.31 shows that genuine extension of todah is accompanied by consecration ('you have now consecrated yourselves to the Lord') and a willing heart, indicating that inner conditions of dedication and voluntary devotion in the giver (here, the assembly/nation) accompany the sincere bringing of thank-offerings.

2Chr.29.31 shows the assembly had first to consecrate themselves before bringing thank offerings, indicating a person must have first undergone consecration/dedication to the Lord before rightly extending todah.

Todah ends where a different sacrificial category begins: it is explicitly distinguished from the burnt offering (2Chr.29.31, 'brought sacrifices and thank offerings...brought burnt offerings') and from the peace offering more generally, being a specific sub-type marked by gratitude/acknowledgment rather than full dedication (burnt offering) or general fellowship (peace offering).

file_lines.text: - Psa 51:9 → 51:10 "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me". **New in v3:** when God is asked to hide his face *from the sin*, the next request places the remedy in **the heart and spirit**. file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The choice is laid out as an offer, with both outcomes (Isa 1:16–20).** *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"willing"* or *"refuse"*; eat, or be eaten. In Isa 7:15 the right choice also ends in eating.

file_lines.section: Choosing has two sides
file_lines.text: The choice is laid out with both its sides and both its ends: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isa 1:16–20).

file_lines.section: What follows the choice
file_lines.text: - The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats *"curds and honey"*, the food of *"everyone who is left in the land"* (Isa 7:15, 22). In the other oracle, *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"* (Isa 1:19).

file_lines.section: 3. The Hebrew: the will is the yes or no to another
file_lines.text: *ʾāḇâ* (H0014) has 52 verses. **50 of them are negated**: "would not", "not willing", "unwilling", "refuse", "would have none". The other two are a question that expects "no" (*"Is the wild ox willing to serve you?"*, Job 39:9) and a condition (*"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*, Isa 1:19).

file_lines.section: 1.3 Refusing God: what was offered, and what it was refused for
file_lines.text: - **Cleansing, after reasoning:** *"Come now, let us reason together … though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow … If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isa 1:18–20). This is the one place in the set where the will is invited with "if". Both ways are set out, as in *Life and death set before a person* (10.7).

observations.text: Fear of a people or a person falls on others. "many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them"; officials "helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them". Of Nebuchadnezzar: "because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whom he would, he killed". Of Ephraim: "When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel, but he incurred guilt through Baal and died". Of the king of Babylon: "Is this the man who made the earth tremble"

Meaning: dread is laid by God, or falls because of his people, and the verses say what it did: the cities did not pursue. Implies: in Rahab, the dread came by hearing, melted heart and spirit, and ends in a confession of God. In Moab, the same dread ends in hiring a curse. Psa 9:20 asks for fear so that the nations know what they are.
